playground.label: First program (uses input)
playground.code:
print('What is your name?')
my_name = input()
print(f'It is good to meet you, {my_name}.')
my_age = int(input('What is your age? '))
print(f'You will be {my_age + 1} in a year.')

findings: Chapter 2 of the 3rd edition introduces the Boolean values True and False, the six comparison operators, the Boolean operators and, or and not, how comparison and Boolean operators mix, the components of flow control - conditions and blocks - and the if, else and elif statements, with two short programs.

The reference documentation makes precise what the chapter leaves informal: and and or return one of their operands rather than a Boolean - x and y returns x if x is false - and evaluate the second operand only when needed; comparisons chain, so x < y <= z means x < y and y <= z; many values besides False count as false, including None, zero of any numeric type and empty sequences; the conditional expression x if C else y chooses a value in one line; and PEP 8 advises against comparing Boolean values to True or False with ==.

For an advanced course, chapter 2 is best taught as decision-making in real Python: truthiness and short-circuit evaluation as working tools, chained comparisons and conditional expressions as idioms, and the match statement as the modern alternative to long elif chains.

Python 3.10 added structural pattern matching: a match statement compares a value against successive case patterns, closer to pattern matching than to the switch statement of C or Java. Python 3.14 adopted PEP 765, which disallows return, break and continue that exit a finally block.
title: Flow control for an advanced course: chapter 2 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Value
nodes.body: Chapter 2 adds a new kind of value, the Boolean, and with it the idea that any value can be tested for truth (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Truth value
nodes.body: Truth is the currency of flow control: every decision a program makes reduces to a true or false value (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Boolean value
nodes.body: The Boolean values True and False are written with a capital letter, and every comparison produces one, so 42 == 42 evaluates to True (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: The two Boolean values, written with a capital letter; the result of every comparison.

nodes.label: Truthiness
nodes.body: Python tests any value for truth, not only Booleans: None, False, zero of any numeric type and empty sequences are false, so bool('') is False while bool('0') is True (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Any value can be tested for truth: None, False, zero and empty sequences are false, so bool('') is False while bool('0') is True.

nodes.label: Comparison
nodes.body: Comparison operators ask a question about two values and answer with a Boolean value (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Equality comparison
nodes.body: Equality comparisons ask whether two values are the same, a different question from assignment's single equals sign (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Equality
nodes.body: The == and != operators compare values, and an integer never equals a string, so 42 == '42' evaluates to False (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: == and != compare values; an integer never equals a string, so 42 == '42' is False.

nodes.label: Ordering comparison
nodes.body: Ordering comparisons ask which of two values comes first, and they combine with Boolean operators into longer conditions (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Ordering
nodes.body: The operators <, >, <= and >= compare order, so (4 < 5) and (5 < 6) evaluates to True (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: <, >, <= and >= compare order and return a Boolean value.

nodes.label: Chained comparison
nodes.body: Comparisons chain, so x < y <= z means x < y and y <= z with y evaluated only once; 1 < 2 < 3 evaluates to True (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: Comparisons chain: x < y <= z means x < y and y <= z, with y evaluated once.

nodes.label: Boolean operation
nodes.body: The Boolean operators and, or and not combine truth values, and the chapter shows them mixed with comparisons in one expression (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Logical operator
nodes.body: Each Boolean operator has a truth table the chapter sets out, and the three together can express any condition a program needs (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: And operator
nodes.body: The and operator is true only when both operands are true, so True and False evaluates to False (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: and is true only when both operands are true.

nodes.label: Or operator
nodes.body: The or operator is true when either operand is true, so True or False evaluates to True (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: or is true when either operand is true.

nodes.label: Not operator
nodes.body: The not operator inverts one Boolean value, so not True evaluates to False (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: not inverts a single Boolean value.

nodes.label: Evaluation
nodes.body: How Boolean operators evaluate matters as much as what they return, because the second operand is sometimes never evaluated at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Short circuit
nodes.body: The and and or operators stop as soon as the answer is known and return one of their operands rather than a Boolean, so '' or 'default' returns 'default' - a common idiom for fallback values (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: and and or stop as soon as the answer is known and return an operand, so '' or 'default' returns 'default'.

nodes.label: Flow control
nodes.body: Flow control decides which lines run and in what order, built from conditions and blocks (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Control structure
nodes.body: The chapter's Components of Flow Control section names the two parts every decision needs: a condition and a block (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Condition
nodes.body: A condition is an expression evaluated for its truth value, and it decides which block of code runs next (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A condition is an expression evaluated for truth to decide which block runs.

nodes.label: Block
nodes.body: A block is a group of lines at the same indentation; Python marks blocks with indentation rather than braces, so indentation is part of the program's meaning (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A block is a group of lines at the same indentation; Python uses indentation, not braces, to mark it.

nodes.label: Branching
nodes.body: The Flow Control Statements section builds branches with if, else and elif, as the Opposite Day and Dishonest Capacity Calculator programs show (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: If statement
nodes.body: An if statement runs its block only when its condition is true, and skips it otherwise (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: if runs its block only when its condition is true.

nodes.label: Elif clause
nodes.body: An elif clause tests a further condition only when every earlier condition was false, so at most one branch of the chain runs (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: elif tests a further condition only when every earlier one was false; at most one branch runs.

nodes.label: Else clause
nodes.body: An else clause runs its block when no earlier condition in the chain was true (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: else runs its block when no earlier condition in the chain was true.

nodes.label: Expression form
nodes.body: Some decisions choose a value rather than run a block, and Python has an expression form for that case (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Conditional expression
nodes.body: The conditional expression x if C else y evaluates the condition first and returns one of two values, so 'even' if 10 % 2 == 0 else 'odd' gives 'even' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: x if C else y chooses between two values in a single expression.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: An advanced course pairs the chapter's if-elif chains with the forms current Python offers for the same decisions (Bucher and Van Rossum, 2020).

nodes.label: Pattern matching
nodes.body: Pattern matching tests a value's shape as well as its value, which elif chains can only imitate (Bucher and Van Rossum, 2020).

nodes.label: Match statement
nodes.body: Since Python 3.10 a match statement compares a value against successive case patterns - closer to pattern matching than to the switch statement of C or Java - and replaces long elif chains (Bucher and Van Rossum, 2020).
nodes.definition: Since Python 3.10 a match statement compares a value against successive case patterns - the modern alternative to a long elif chain.

nodes.label: Style
nodes.body: Style guidance keeps conditions readable, and the conventions for Boolean tests are among the most often broken (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

nodes.label: Boolean comparison style
nodes.body: PEP 8 advises testing a Boolean directly - if greeting: - instead of comparing it to True with == (Van Rossum et al., 2001); Python 3.14 also tightened flow control by adopting PEP 765, which disallows return, break and continue that exit a finally block (Katriel and Coghlan, 2024).
nodes.example: if greeting: rather than if greeting == True:
nodes.definition: PEP 8 advises testing a Boolean directly instead of comparing it to True or False with ==.
